# 3D Western

3D Western is a student club at Western University that runs free makerspaces for students, in partnership with Morrissette Entrepreneurship. I joined as a Software Developer in Sep 2025 and was promoted to VP of Data/ML for May to Aug 2026, alongside my TeraGo internship. The club was building a print service where students submit jobs through its website, and anyone can upload an STL, so it needed a classifier to stop explicit or weapon-like models.

3D Western > tl;dr
(experience, Sep 2025 to Aug 2026, role: VP of Data/ML (promoted from Software Developer))

- There was no labelled set of 3D models to choose one with, so the data team built one. Teammates wrote the preprocessing pipeline and render scripts. I got them working together, rendered and verified the full set, and fixed the bugs that broke the run: 2,559 clean labelled models from 4,620 scraped files.
- Our best small local model, Qwen3-VL-2B with the binary_v7 prompt, matched the labels on 84.2% of models with the filename included, and still missed about 21% of what it should flag. Our best image-only number is 76.9%, from the earlier v6 prompt. It isn't ready to ship.
- I built the eval that ruled out Shieldstral, a 3B safety model. Reviewing the pipeline, I noticed it only verified labels we already had, while real uploads arrive unlabelled, so we turned toward classification. I handed off a smoke-tested multi-model benchmark for a cluster run.

3D Western > The team and my role
(experience, Sep 2025 to Aug 2026, role: VP of Data/ML (promoted from Software Developer))

Alongside the frontend, backend and infrastructure teams, the data team was two VPs and two developers. The other VP was also VP of Backend, so I ended up running most of the day-to-day: reviewing PRs, testing changes locally and getting them merged. It was my first dev team outside two-day hackathons, run on Jira tickets and a kanban board, and I liked working that way.

3D Western > Building the dataset
(experience, Sep 2025 to Aug 2026, role: VP of Data/ML (promoted from Software Developer))

A teammate's pipeline drops exact duplicates by SHA-256 hash (802), renders each model in Blender, has a cloud VLM check each render against its scraped folder label, and exports the matches. The scraped folders were safe, unsafe and grey. Unsafe held only nudity, and grey held the other categories we'd want to stop: in the clean set, guns, knives, swords and gestures. For a print gate, both count as "flag".

From 4,620 scraped files to 2,559 clean ones. 1,259 went to review: 735 mismatches, 522 uncertain, and 2 matches that didn't make the export. Two charts. Left, a funnel: 4,620 STL files discovered, 3,818 unique after removing 802 duplicates, and 2,559 in the clean dataset. Right, stacked bars: of the 3,818 checked, 735 were label mismatches and 522 were uncertain. The clean 2,559 split into 1,091 safe, 336 unsafe and 1,132 grey.

3D Western > Building the dataset
(experience, Sep 2025 to Aug 2026, role: VP of Data/ML (promoted from Software Developer))

My part:

- I reviewed the branch against its ticket. It met all five acceptance criteria, but every render failed: it asked for Blender's EEVEE_NEXT engine, which doesn't exist in Blender 5.1.1. I switched it to WORKBENCH, which I'd measured at about 3 times faster per view than the Cycles setup in the render scripts.

- I merged it with a teammate's new render branch. It merged cleanly, then broke in four places, which I fixed: the manifest was never written, so contact sheets failed; the preset flag was ignored; grid layouts never cleaned up their tiles; and the contact-sheet glob looked for the wrong filenames.

- I added parallel workers, a resolution flag and output renaming to the batch renderer, then rendered the set with zero failures. Each model became one labelled 768×568 contact sheet of six 256×256 views, about 258 Gemini image tokens, against about 1,032 for the same sheet with 800 px views.

3D Western > Building the dataset
(experience, Sep 2025 to Aug 2026, role: VP of Data/ML (promoted from Software Developer))

- I added parallel workers, a resolution flag and output renaming to the batch renderer, then rendered the set with zero failures. Each model became one labelled 768×568 contact sheet of six 256×256 views, about 258 Gemini image tokens, against about 1,032 for the same sheet with 800 px views.

- I ran the full verification of 3,818 models. The VLM kept matching the "grey" label to the grey clay of the render, so I made the prompt say labels describe the content. Results were only saved at the end, so one restart cost about 50 minutes of calls; I added per-sample saves and resume.

That first review is also where I noted the pipeline only checks models against labels they already have. Real uploads have none, so production has to classify. I rewrote the production prompt as a classifier around a teammate's taxonomy prompt, the best in a 1,440-call prompt evaluation.

The 2,559-model benchmark set. Unsafe is the nudity folder and grey is guns, knives, swords and gestures. Both count as flag, so 1,468 of the 2,559 (57%) should be flagged. Donut chart of the 2,559-sample benchmark set. Safe 42.6%, guns 33.0%, nudity 13.1%, swords 5.7%, knives 4.2%, gestures 1.4%. Counted as a binary task, 57% is unsafe.

3D Western > Benchmarking small vision models
(experience, Sep 2025 to Aug 2026, role: VP of Data/ML (promoted from Software Developer))

We wanted a model small enough for the club to run itself, starting with Qwen3-VL-2B. The data team iterated on prompts on a 30-sample dev set, where v5 peaked at 90%. With so few samples, the versions that count are v6 and the later v7, run on all 2,559 clean models.

Every number below is agreement with folder labels a cloud VLM confirmed, so the clean set leans toward models a VLM already recognizes. Prompts and thresholds were chosen on this same set too, with no held-out split, so I'd read all of them as optimistic.

binary_v6 on the clean set, with the filename. It flags 4.2% of safe models and misses 30.7% of the ones it should flag. Dashboard for Qwen3-VL-2B with the binary_v6 prompt on 2,559 samples. Accuracy 80.6%, safe precision 69.9%, false positive rate 4.2%, false negative rate 30.7%, about 1.5 seconds per sample. Per-category accuracy: safe 96%, nudity 81%, guns 67%, knives 48%, swords 70%, gestures 74%. Filename plus size scores 80.6% against 76.9% for vision only.

3D Western > Benchmarking small vision models
(experience, Sep 2025 to Aug 2026, role: VP of Data/ML (promoted from Software Developer))

binary_v6 on the clean set, with the filename. It flags 4.2% of safe models and misses 30.7% of the ones it should flag. Dashboard for Qwen3-VL-2B with the binary_v6 prompt on 2,559 samples. Accuracy 80.6%, safe precision 69.9%, false positive rate 4.2%, false negative rate 30.7%, about 1.5 seconds per sample. Per-category accuracy: safe 96%, nudity 81%, guns 67%, knives 48%, swords 70%, gestures 74%. Filename plus size scores 80.6% against 76.9% for vision only.

binary_v6 sees the render plus the file's name and size, which scored 80.6% against 76.9% from the image alone. But a scraped filename can give the answer away, and uploaders name files anything, so 76.9% is our realistic baseline.

binary_v7, a later revision, cut misses from 450 to 307 at the cost of more false flags (97, up from 46), and matched the labels on 84.2% of models. It also sees the filename, and these results don't include an image-only run of it.

3D Western > Shieldstral vs Qwen
(experience, Sep 2025 to Aug 2026, role: VP of Data/ML (promoted from Software Developer))

We kept Qwen3-VL-2B with binary_v7: the highest agreement and less than half of Shieldstral's false flags, for 26 more misses. Two charts on all 2,559 samples. Accuracy: Qwen3-VL-2B binary_v6 80.6%, Qwen3-VL-2B binary_v7 84.2% (kept), Shieldstral-1.0-3B at threshold 0.02 80.7%. Errors: binary_v6 46 false positives and 450 false negatives, binary_v7 97 and 307, Shieldstral 212 and 281.

Shieldstral-1.0-3B is made for image safety. I wrote an eval harness for it on llama.cpp that scores its probability of "yes" from the same render and filename. At the default threshold of 0.5 it got 56.7%. A sweep over the saved scores reached 80.7% at 0.02, again tuned on the same set. It missed 26 fewer than binary_v7 (281 against 307), but it produced more than twice the false flags to review (212 against 97) and it's a bigger model to host, so we kept Qwen.

3D Western > Shieldstral vs Qwen
(experience, Sep 2025 to Aug 2026, role: VP of Data/ML (promoted from Software Developer))

Shieldstral-1.0-3B is made for image safety. I wrote an eval harness for it on llama.cpp that scores its probability of "yes" from the same render and filename. At the default threshold of 0.5 it got 56.7%. A sweep over the saved scores reached 80.7% at 0.02, again tuned on the same set. It missed 26 fewer than binary_v7 (281 against 307), but it produced more than twice the false flags to review (212 against 97) and it's a bigger model to host, so we kept Qwen.

To see why Shieldstral needed such a low threshold, I ran a small control. A real photo of an AK-47 scored 0.90 for unsafe, and a clay render of an AK-47 part scored 0.20. My best explanation is domain shift: its encoder learned from photos, and clay renders look like generic mechanical shapes. Two images don't prove it, but scoring renders and photos of the same objects across categories would.

3D Western > Handoff
(experience, Sep 2025 to Aug 2026, role: VP of Data/ML (promoted from Software Developer))

I got all four open PRs merged to main, then reviewed the multi-model benchmark harness and runbook for Nibi, a research compute cluster. I fixed four issues, like a missing path that failed silently, smoke-tested it end to end and handed it off with a 30-sample check to run before the full sweep.

3D Western > What I'd do next
(experience, Sep 2025 to Aug 2026, role: VP of Data/ML (promoted from Software Developer))

Still open when my term ended in Aug 2026:

- Build a held-out split and rerun v7 on it, with and without the filename.
- Check whether Qwen's saved scores have the same threshold headroom Shieldstral had.
- Sort the flagged models into bad source labels and verifier mistakes, and reuse them as a harder test set.
- Finish the switch to classifying uploads, then wire it into the print form.

(page, Apr 2026 (approx.) to present)

Built at Hack the 6ix 2026, AWARE runs every model on one $80 Arduino UNO Q, using the board's Adreno GPU through ONNX Runtime QNN. The LLM only turns plain-English commands into rules through a `create_rule()` call; a deterministic parser compiles them, and a rules engine checks them every 500 ms without the LLM. Details in [AWARE](/knowledgebase/projects/aware.md).

AgenticArmy > Description
(project, Mar 2026, role: team, status: shipped)

AgenticArmy answers a practical question: how do you run multiple "coder agents" in parallel without them constantly conflicting, duplicating work, or losing context?

### Workflow

1. **Human provides goal** - High-level process, success metrics

2. **Planning agent runs** - Finds ways the goal can be implemented

3. **Human approves/denies plan** - If denied, return to step 2

4. **Task coordinator agent runs** - Splits tasks among agents

5. **Conflict analysis agent runs** - Assigns conflict scores based on likelihood of overwriting each other's work

6. **Coding agents run** - Tasks completed in isolated environments

7. **Merge agent runs** - Merges individual agent commits

8. **QA agent runs** - Tests code for functionality

### Key Features

- **Conflict Analysis**: Anticipates coding agent disagreements before they happen

- **Human-in-the-Loop**: Human intervention only for goal setting and plan approval

- **Similarity Scoring**: Calculates possibility of code overlap for reliable merges

- **State Machine**: Supports loopbacks (plan rejection, conflict risk too high, merge failure, QA failure)

AWARE > How it works

A camera, microphone and sensors feed an always-on perception pipeline. A plain-English command goes through the on-device language model to become a rule. The rules engine checks every rule every 500 milliseconds and drives a speaker, LEDs, Telegram alerts and video clips.

4. Action. Piper TTS on a Bluetooth speaker, LEDs, servo or relay control, Telegram alerts, video clips, and live dashboard updates.

Campus > What I built

It's a solo project, so everything below is mine.

- LMS sync with Playwright, MFA login included, into SQLite and a local file store.
- sha256 change detection, so unchanged files are not downloaded again.
- Hybrid retrieval: embedding search, cross-encoder reranking, and a lexical SQL prefilter.
- A fix for exact phrases that scored below the semantic cutoff. They now go through the lexical path.

Campus > How it works
(project, Aug 2026 to present, role: solo, status: active)

Brightspace syncs into SQLite and a local file store. Those files are split into an index of chunks. Retrieval reads the index and feeds an agent with twenty tools, which answers questions and writes every change to an audit log with the before and after state.

1. Sync. Playwright signs in and pulls course content. Files with an unchanged sha256 are skipped.
2. Index. Course files are split into chunks.
3. Retrieve. A SQL prefilter catches exact phrases, embedding search finds related chunks, and a cross-encoder reranks them.
4. Answer. The agent picks from its tools to search, read files, or change notes and due dates.
5. Audit. Every write is logged with its before and after state.

# ferret

Local-first semantic file search. Ferret indexes text, images and PDF pages into one local SQLite file and searches it by meaning, keywords or filename, from the terminal, from fzf, from Quickshell or from an agent. It ships as one static Rust binary, with no daemon and no GUI.

ferret > How it works
(project, Oct 2026 (approx.), role: solo)

1. Walk the configured roots, honouring gitignore, hidden files, size caps and include or exclude globs, and report every skip.
2. Extract text chunks, image pixels and PDF pages, the last as text plus an optional raster per page.
3. Embed through an OpenAI-compatible embedding server. The default is a local `llama-server` running EmbeddingGemma; ferret itself never loads model weights.
4. Search hybrid: vector similarity, keyword and filename, fused with reciprocal rank fusion, with filters applied in SQL before ranking.

ferret > What it does
(project, Oct 2026 (approx.), role: solo)

- Indexes text, images, PDFs, audio and video. Audio and video become segments (30 seconds and 10 seconds by default) embedded through the model's audio and video encoders, with no transcription, and stay searchable with plain text queries.

(project, May 2026 to present, role: solo, status: active)

I used to run a Debian Docker Compose homelab and a separate local AI setup. Both drifted from their config over time. I started building my own agent for NixOS configuration first (AgntOS), got impatient, and switched to NixOS with Hermes Agent instead. It works really well.

NixOS homelab > What I built
(project, May 2026 to present, role: solo, status: active)

I designed and built everything below. The agents edit config inside it, and I review every change before it applies.

- Moved both old setups to NixOS one service at a time, into one flake.
- Split services into modules by role: infrastructure, access, media, AI and monitoring.
- Put every service behind Caddy, reachable only over my private Tailscale network.
- Hardened containers: dropped capabilities, no-new-privileges, resource limits.
- Secrets encrypted in git with sops-nix, decrypted at boot to tmpfs.
- A self-hosted AI stack: Open WebUI, a Bifrost gateway between local and cloud models, crawl4ai, DeGoog search and Whisper.
- Two MCP servers. trawl does web search and page reading in one tool. Brightspace MCP exposes my courses, assignments, grades and announcements.

- llama.cpp on the laptop as a local model provider.

NixOS homelab > How it works
(project, May 2026 to present, role: solo, status: active)

Hermes Agent is an AI agent from Nous Research that works through tools and saved skills.

I ask an agent for a change. The agent edits the NixOS config and never touches the running system by hand. I approve, a safe-rebuild guard applies it, and if the build fails it rolls back to the last good build.

1. I ask an agent for a change. The flow profile works on the laptop. The homelab profile reaches the server over SSH.
2. The agent edits the config. It never changes the running system by hand.
3. I approve. nixos-safe-rebuild applies it and rolls back if the build fails.
4. If a bad change gets through anyway, I boot the previous NixOS generation.
5. Subagents take the bigger investigations. A weekly curator prunes the skill library and backs up what it removes.
6. Uptime Kuma checks every service each minute, Netdata tracks metrics, and ntfy sends alerts.

VitalSign > Description

VitalSign turns sign language into speech and carries the emotion from your face into the voice. It helps Deaf and non-verbal users communicate more naturally in situations where interpreters aren't available.

### Inspiration

Many accessibility tools focus on word translation and miss emotional context. VitalSign preserves both meaning and emotion, helping Deaf and non-verbal users communicate more naturally.

### What It Does

1. **Real-time ASL Translation**

- Users sign in front of webcam

- System detects gestures using MediaPipe

- Converts to text in real-time

2. **Emotion Detection**

- face-api.js analyzes facial expressions

- Detects emotional state alongside signs

- Provides context for more natural communication

3. **AI Text Refinement**

- Cohere AI refines detected gestures into natural sentences

- Fixes grammar and adds context

- Makes communication more fluid

4. **Emotion-Aware Speech**

- ElevenLabs converts text to speech

- Adjusts voice tone based on detected emotions

- Preserves emotional nuance in spoken output

5. **Web-Based Solution**

- No special hardware required
